graduation_requirements.raw_text: To receive a diploma from Mt. Mansfield Union High School, students must demonstrate proficiency in the following Graduation Areas: Literacy, Mathematical Content and Practices, Scientific Inquiry and Content Knowledge, Global Citizenship, Physical and Health Education, Artistic Expression, and Transferable Skills and fulfill the requirements of the Advisory Program. They demonstrate proficiency in these areas by demonstrating proficiency on each of the Proficiency Based Graduation Requirements that are aligned with the Graduation Areas. While school counselors perform periodic checks of student standing in regards to their performance in meeting the requirements, students are responsible for knowing their own standing and progress toward meeting graduation requirements. The Advisory Program at MMU builds a greater sense of community and creates a school culture in which each student is known well and supported by an adult advisor and a small group of diverse peers. Students are randomly assigned to an advisor and group. All students are required to participate in advisory each year they are at MMU. They will be awarded a pass based upon attendance and PLP completion. This one semester course is designed as a way for seniors to learn some of the essential skills of adulthood. Topics will include job exploration, resumes, budgeting, saving, investing, as well as other imperative life skills such as negotiating with roommates and addressing physical and mental wellness. This course is required for all 12th graders.

courses.description: English 9 is a course designed to provide a strong, academic foundation in literacy that will prepare students for writing, reading, and research in all high school classes. In this course students develop their skills through extensive practice with multiple forms of writing, including literary and informational text analysis, narratives, and informational writing. Readings include classic texts such as To Kill a Mockingbird and Romeo and Juliet as well as selections of non-fiction, informational texts, poetry, and short stories. Students have the opportunity to discuss and analyze their reading using both live and electronic formats. Research skills are a major focus of the course and students conduct both short and extended research products, including written essays and presentations.

The goal of this course is to explore our cultural foundations by reading a range of culturally significant literature, examining the lasting influence of the universal themes that emerge from our reading, and considering the importance of stories and storytellers both in shaping and conveying those themes and in providing cultural continuity. The first semester begins with an examination of Homer’s epic poems The Iliad and the Odyssey, contrasted with contemporary fiction and non-fiction texts that respond to the thematic assumptions of the ancient Greeks. In the second semester, more extensive writing is included as students engage in the Making of the Artist project, in which they will explore the relationship between an artist and his or her culture in a research paper and a presentation, and as they continue to synthesize multiple texts thematically and historically. The course is designed to prepare students to meet the Language Proficiency, which assesses students’ control of grammar in various forms of writing.
courses.prerequisites: English 9 and recommendation of English teacher; strong analytical and note-making skills.
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Research; Language

courses.description: The goal of this course is to explore our cultural foundations by reading a range of culturally significant literature and by examining the lasting influence of the universal themes that emerge from our reading. Readings include selections from mythology and the Bible, Julius Caesar, Fahrenheit 451, and Animal Farm. In addition to these major works, there will be selections of non-fiction as part of Non-Fiction Friday, a discussion format in which students lead each other in critical discourse on relevant and engaging topics. The course is designed to prepare students to meet the Language Proficiency which assesses students’ control of grammar and sound style in various forms of writing. Through writing, students will develop techniques for the integration of primary and secondary sources, and the synthesis of the course’s overarching themes. A centerpiece of the course is the Making of the Artist project, in which each student explores the relationship between an artist and his or her culture in a research paper and a presentation.

courses.description: Advanced Placement English Language & Composition is a college level course designed to further students’ reading, writing and critical thinking skills through in-depth study of the English language, particularly language used to argue and persuade (rhetoric). Students read a variety of nonfiction texts, analyzing both their meaning and the effect of the rhetorical strategies used to create that meaning. Students then learn to apply similar rhetorical strategies to their own writing. Thematic units invite students to engage in discussion and writing about issues including the role of the individual in the community, politics, education, social responsibility, and the interplay of language and culture. In order to be successful in this course, participants will have demonstrated a commitment to independent work and study as the course requires students to spend a good deal of time reading and deconstructing college-level texts as well as writing and rewriting argument, synthesis (researched-based) and rhetorical analysis essays with control and purpose. The goal of the course is to prepare students for college writing in a variety of disciplines as well as to provide an enriching experience in the study of writing and language while engaging in the world around them.

courses.description: America’s rich and constantly evolving literature has served to both reflect and energize the cultural evolution of our country. This college preparatory class uses a variety of texts including novels, short stories, poetry, and nonfiction to explore themes, conflicts, and beliefs that have defined and shaped the American experience. Students examine the socio-cultural and historical influences that have shaped America’s writers, American thought, and the role of the American literary voice. Writing, vocabulary study, and the development of research skills for college reading and writing are an integral part of the course, and students take an active role in shaping class conversations and the direction of study. Major texts are chosen for student interest and exploration of the following themes: American Dream/American Identity, Freedom and Oppression, The Life Well Lived, and Real vs. Ideal. Students will also fulfill the Core Values element of their PLP in this class.
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Writing; Research

courses.course_name: Advanced Placement English Literature and Composition
courses.description: This course is for those college preparatory students who are ready for college-level English assignments and have a special interest in literature and writing. The course places emphasis on analysis of literature, development of the ability to read critically, improvement in writing skills through continuous practices, and the practice and improvement of critical discourse. During two periods called Boot Camp (one for short fiction and one for poetry) students will prepare essays for each class period and in addition will have many other writing opportunities. Outside of short fiction and poetry, full length works have included King Lear, Exit West, Native Son, The God of Small Things, Hamlet, Death of a Salesman, A Doll House, The Glass Menagerie, 1984, The Color Purple, The Catcher in the Rye, and The Handmaid’s Tale. Students are required to take the AP exam, and summer work consists of reading three assigned novels or plays and writing three essays. This course has open enrollment. Seniors who wish to challenge themselves in a college-level English course may enroll. Students should discuss their potential success in the course with their current instructors and must talk with their counselor before enrolling in 12AP.

courses.course_name: Visions of the Future: Dystopia, Utopia, & Science Fiction
courses.description: Imagine a world controlled by machines…or clones…or hybrid animals…or an evil dictator. Is a world like that even possible – scientifically, politically, or socially? As our society continues to progress, how many of these stories will remain fiction? (Think The Hunger Games, 1984 by George Orwell, or Black Mirror.) Explore different attempts to create a perfect world and where we can see reflections of those ideas in our contemporary society through fiction, non-fiction, podcasts, and film.

courses.description: Crime is complicated. This course attempts to unravel our relationship with crime by analyzing the stories behind the crimes. Through fiction and nonfiction, songs, film, podcasts, and other media, explore the essential questions of: Nature or nurture? What motivates a person to commit a crime? How is justice served? What role do truth and memory play in understanding a crime? What motivates individuals to do socially unacceptable, horrific, or unexplainable things? Stories will be told from multiple perspectives: from the victims, perpetrators, media, witnesses, the law…. A good companion course to American Law, Psychology, or Forensics. WARNING: This course has disturbing and dark content.

courses.description: Why do movies and films have such a captivating power to tell a story? Film is a unique art that combines a variety of visual and audio elements to appeal to its viewers. This class will start by seeking to identify and use the various tools that filmmakers use to tell their stories while engaging an audience. The Storytelling Power of Film will also spend time exploring film genres and how time periods may influence the style, as well as how the tools that certain types of films, i.e., action, film noir, westerns, comedies, use to tell their story. We will watch a variety of films and film excerpts. Some are considered “classics” while others are more contemporary. The class will provide several opportunities for some students to use the tools of film to tell their own stories.

courses.description: Comedy as Commentary and the Language of Laughter: What is humor and what is it for? From memoirs to memes, this class will explore the form and function of laughter/comedy/humor. Organized thematically, it investigates the following essential questions: ● What makes something funny? ● What are the different types of humor? ● How can comedy be a powerful communication tool? ● What changes and what stays the same when comedy is looked at historically, culturally, or through different perspectives?

courses.description: Our world relies on clear, effective communication. Our ability to communicate effectively can build connections, influence decision making, and initiate change. This course looks to identify and develop the skills that make for effective and impactful oral and written communication. Students will find that this course builds on and enhances a variety of skills they have encountered in other classes, while also increasing the confidence and poise inherent to effective communication. Speech habits, nonverbal communication, audience engagement, and persuasion are all areas of focus, and are done so in a collaborative, supportive atmosphere. Students are encouraged to identify individual areas of growth and challenge, and have many opportunities to develop in those, and other areas. Activities are wide ranging, and include persuasive presentations, TED-style talks, goal setting, storytelling, tributes, and skills and strategies to apply to a variety of practical and impromptu speaking situations. Your confidence will grow, your effectiveness will be refined, and you will have a whole lot of fun.

courses.description: The exciting part of creative writing is the sense of wonder at what emerges when you put words to your imagination, ideas, experiences, and observations. This course is about tapping into the art form of the written word. Through daily journaling and the drafting process, we’ll experiment with different forms of writing including poetry, short stories, and a variety of nonfiction genres. Grading is NOT based on talent. Instead you will be assessed on effort, improvement, and participation, including your willingness to write, to revise, to take risks, and to give and receive constructive feedback. The workshop process is an essential component to this class so you must be willing to share your work.

courses.description: This course begins with a study of limits and their use with continuity theorems. We’ll then look at differential calculus and its applications. The final topic to be covered is integral calculus. We’ll look at the anti-derivative and its applications. We’ll study techniques of integration, the Fundamental Theorem, and applications of the definite integral. Students taking this AP course are also expected to take the AP exam given each May. College credit for the course will depend on this exam grade, as well as the policies of the college to which the student is applying.
courses.prerequisites: Math 3 Honors or recommendation of Math 3/3H teacher.

courses.description: If you have big ideas and an interest in using technology and creativity to realize those ideas and solve problems, Computer Science Principles is for you! AP Computer Science Principles is a year-long course which introduces students to the foundational concepts of computer science and challenges them to explore how computing and technology can impact the world. Colleges consider this to be equivalent to the first semester of an introductory course for non-STEM and liberal arts majors. It is expected that all students take the AP Examination, which includes the submission of classwork in addition to the multiple choice examination in May. There is lots of partner work, so it might be fun to sign up with a friend! There are a lot of myths and misconceptions about what computer science is and isn’t. Let’s set the record straight: ● Computer science isn’t posting pictures, sending email or searching the Internet. You can use it to pursue your interests, showcase your creativity, and even make a difference in your community. ● It’s not about sitting in front of a computer alone, typing code all day (and night). It is about using one elaborate tool to solve real-world problems. ● Teamwork is often essential to finding those solutions, and each team member’s contributions are valuable to the end goal. ● You don’t have to be a math whiz to understand computer science. ● Even though this is an AP class, you do not need prior experience programming. ● Studying computer science doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll be a programmer. It can lead to hundreds of career choices, from engineering and animation to medicine and music.

courses.description: This course is the fourth in the MMU traditional math curriculum. It is for the student who wishes to continue taking a traditional mathematics course and it has been designed to prepare students for college mathematics courses. We will be working from numerous resources including the textbook Precalculus: A Graphing Approach (Holt) and the textbook Calculus: Graphical, Numerical, Algebraic, 4th Edition (Prentice Hall). Topics covered in this course will include: 1. Rational & Radical Expressions & Functions 2. Trigonometry functions 3. Sequences & Matrices 4. Introduction to Differential Calculus

Students taking the AP class will have additional projects designed to prepare them for the AP test in May. A graphing calculator is required. courses.description: This course builds on the topics studied in Math 1 and Math 2. Building on their work with linear, quadratic, and exponential functions, students extend their repertoire of functions to include polynomial, rational, and radical functions. Students work closely with the expressions that define the functions, and continue to expand and hone their abilities to model situations and to solve equations, including solving quadratic equations over the set of complex numbers and solving exponential equations using the properties of logarithms. Students also see how the visual displays and summary statistics they learned in earlier grades relate to different types of data and to probability distributions. They identify different ways of collecting data and the role that randomness and careful design play in the conclusions that can be drawn. Our curriculum integrates technology, and a graphing calculator is required (the suggested model is the TI-84). The Mathematical Practice Standards apply throughout the course and, together with the content standards, prescribe that students experience mathematics as a coherent, useful, and logical subject that makes use of their ability to make sense of problem situations.

courses.description: Math 2 is the class that the majority of MMU’s second year students will be enrolled in, and has been designed to support the recommendations provided in Appendix A of the Common Core State Standards. The fundamental purpose of the first semester of Math 2 includes units of learning designed to introduce and extend understanding of quadratic, rational and radical relationships. Second semester is a continuation of geometric topics and skills introduced in Math 1 with focus on dilations, similarity, right triangles, and circles. A unit of study of basic probability is also included. The Mathematical Practice Standards apply throughout the course and, together with the content standards, prescribe that students experience mathematics as a coherent, useful, and logical subject that makes use of their ability to make sense of problem situations.

The fundamental purpose of Math 1 includes units of learning designed to deepen and extend understanding of linear relationships, in part by contrasting them with exponential phenomena, and in part by applying linear models to data that exhibit a linear trend. Math 1 introduces properties and theorems involving congruent figures and isometric transformations. The final unit in the course ties together the algebraic and geometric ideas studied. The Mathematical Practice Standards apply throughout the course and, together with the content standards, prescribe that students experience mathematics as a coherent, useful, and logical subject that makes use of their ability to make sense of problem situations.

courses.description: Math 1 Honors is a rich, rigorous and fast paced course designed as the first in a series of three with the intent to prepare students for future AP courses, and to challenge students to work beyond their comfort zone in mathematics and problem solving. The class is designed for learners who can independently use a variety of mathematical strategies to persevere through complex math problems. Students will need to apply previous knowledge and integrate new ideas with fluency. The course covers algebra topics seen in Math 1 and Math 2 as well as some from Math 3 consistent with the Common Core State Standards. These include work with linear, quadratic and other polynomial and piecewise functions. Additionally, the course includes a comprehensive study of geometric congruence, coordinate geometry, and mathematical reasoning (proof) and an introductory unit on descriptive statistics.

courses.description: This course prepares students for Algebra, and operates differently than other mathematics courses at Mt. Mansfield. The course covers Pre-Algebra and Pre-Tech topics including operations with fractions, decimals, ratios, and percents; operations with signed numbers; working with polynomial expressions; solving linear and systems of equations and inequalities; data analysis; basic geometry; probability; graphs of linear equations; polynomial operations and factoring. This course is different in several ways: ● Students spend most of their time working on topics that they need to develop, rather than having all students work on the same lesson at the same time. ● Placement into Math 1 is dependent upon a student demonstrating a mastery of required topics. This mastery will occur at different rates for different students; some students may require additional time to complete these requirements. ● Grading for this course is based upon continuous mastery of requirements and work habits. Upon successful mastery of the topics covered in this course and teacher recommendation, the student will be able to enroll in Math 1 for the following year.

They then move on to learn relevant knowledge and hands-on skills related to a wide variety of topics essential in modern industry, including: Robotic operation and programming; AC/DC electricity; pneumatic power; electrical relay control; computer-aided design and manufacturing; CNC machine operation and programming; and factory emulation on the SkillBoss and Mechatronics equipment. This class develops problem solving skills in a fun, interactive, team-based, hands-on, self-regulated environment. Field trips are taken to local manufacturing and related sites to examine, evaluate and experience advanced manufacturing in the real world. This course can lead to a continuation of advanced manufacturing and other engineering and computer science studies or careers.

courses.description: AP Physics 1 is a college-level physics class that addresses topics usually covered in one year of introductory college-level physics. There is extensive exploratory lab work, as well as conceptual and mathematical modeling of concepts. Topics of study will include Statics and Vectors, Kinematics, Newtonian Mechanics, The Conservation Laws, Circular Motion and Gravitation, Waves and Oscillations, and Fluids. The course is designed to prepare students for the AP Physics 1 exam, which is offered in the spring.
courses.prerequisites: Math 3 and recommendation from a science teacher.
courses.notes: Lab Included (AP Physics 1) | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Scale, Proportion, and Quantity; Energy and Matter; Scientific and Engineering Practices

courses.description: The topics in the course include the various types of motion, forces, energy and momentum, optics, waves, sound and electricity. A significant part of the class time will involve experimentation, and material will be presented in both a traditional way and through inquiry.
courses.prerequisites: Math 1, concurrent Math 2, and recommendation of a science teacher.
courses.notes: Lab Included | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Scale, Proportion, and Quantity; Energy and Matter; Scientific and Engineering Practices

courses.description: This one semester course explores the different celestial bodies in the night sky, star and planetary motion, space travel and space probes, current topics in astronomy like exoplanets and Mars exploration, as well as key concepts in the history of astronomy. Students will apply physics concepts to the different celestial bodies, as well as understand and explain the different patterns that help astronomers understand our place in the cosmos. Attendance at multiple evening star gazing sessions is required.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Math 1 and recommendation of science teacher.
courses.notes: One Semester; Lab Included, Grades 10-12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Scale, Proportion, and Quantity

courses.description: AP Chemistry builds on concepts from the first year Chemistry or Chemistry Honors course, including structure and properties of matter and chemical reactions. The course continues the study of matter through additional topics: kinetics, equilibrium, acids and bases, thermochemistry, and electrochemistry. This course is intended for students considering a major in science in college, and will prepare students for the AP exam in the spring. Laboratory work is extensive.
courses.prerequisites: Have met the PBGRs associated with Chemistry or Chemistry Honors and have passed Math 3 as well as recommendation of science teacher.
courses.notes: Lab Included | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Scale, Proportion, and Quantity; Energy and Matter; Scientific and Engineering Practices

courses.description: The AP Biology course is designed to be the equivalent of a college introductory biology course. This course differs significantly from the usual high school course in biology with respect to the range and depth of topics covered, the kind of laboratory work done by students, and the time and effort required of students. Topics include chemistry of life, cell biology, cellular energetics, heredity, evolution, diversity of organisms and ecology. Upon completion of the course, students who qualify on the AP Biology Examination have the opportunity to receive college credit and register for upper-level courses in biology in their first year of college.
courses.prerequisites: Have met the PBGRs associated with Biology, concurrently enrolled in or have already completed chemistry and/or recommendation from a science teacher.
courses.notes: Lab Included | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Cause and Effect; Structure and Function

courses.description: In this one semester course students will focus on applying the Engineering process to design, build and test solutions to real world problems. As part of a design team, students will apply skills and knowledge from engineering, technology, math, arts, and science to develop creative solutions and models. Students will learn to design and produce 3D and 2D models and to use equipment in our MakerSpace. An emphasis will be placed on documenting the design process.
courses.prerequisites: Recommendation of science teacher.
courses.notes: One Semester; Grades 10-12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Scientific and Engineering Practices

courses.description: This one-semester course further develops skills and methods from Engineering & Design Principles 1. Students will use 3D printing, laser cutter, robotics, and CNC cutting machines to continue to develop engineering skills. This course will continue to emphasize the iterative design and Engineering problem-solving skills introduced in Engineering & Design Principles 1. Participation and group work are important parts of this course. Project units may vary, but could include: small aquaponic systems; scale models of wind turbines; solar-powered mini-vehicles and robotics, as well as extensive use of design and build tools.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Engineering & Design Principles 1 or teacher permission.
courses.notes: One Semester; Grades 10-12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Scientific and Engineering Practices

courses.description: See description below under Chemistry 4140. Chemistry Honors demands more math and in-depth coverage of the areas described in Chemistry.
courses.prerequisites: Science teacher recommendation and concurrent enrollment in Math 3 or higher class.
courses.notes: Lab Included | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Scale, Proportion, and Quantity; Energy and Matter; Scientific and Engineering Practices

courses.description: Chemistry is a lab-based foundation for any college physical-science majors. Matter, energy and their changes are the focus of chemistry. Beginning with the math and language of chemistry, students, through discussion and experimentation, will explore reactions, stoichiometry, the atom, periodic trends, bonding, gasses, and acids and bases. There is a focus on understanding and explaining different patterns found on the chemical level, as well as being able to explain matter and energy both qualitatively and quantitatively. There is extensive lab work, often through inquiry-based activities. Chemistry Honors demands more math and in-depth coverage of the areas described in Chemistry.
courses.prerequisites: Math 1 and recommendation of current science teacher.
courses.notes: Lab Included; Chemistry Honors (4120) is a separate listing | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Scale, Proportion, and Quantity; Energy and Matter; Scientific and Engineering Practices

courses.description: This year-long course will focus on chemistry and physics concepts that are all around us. One semester of this course focuses on chemistry topics including chemical and physical properties of matter, chemical reactions, conservation of matter, and gasses. One semester of the class is devoted to physics topics including motion, force, energy and momentum, sound, light and electricity. The class is hands-on with lab work, inquiry-based activities, projects, and real world activities.
courses.prerequisites: Recommendation of science teacher.
courses.notes: Lab Included | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Scale, Proportion, and Quantity; Energy and Matter; Scientific and Engineering Practices

courses.description: This course covers the main systems in the human body: cardiovascular, respiratory, nervous, immune, digestive, and others. Students also study related diseases, medical terminology, treatment approaches, and how personal choices influence individual health. Interactions between health, disease, and society are considered, both historically and in the present. Emphases include relationships between anatomical structures and their functions, and connections between symptoms and underlying causes. This course offers enough detail to provide a good introduction for students who intend to continue into health-related college fields, but is also suitable for students with general interest in the human body. Activities include: dissections; lab exercises; microscope work; blood typing and analysis; and fitness-related activities with heart monitors.
courses.prerequisites: Have met the PBGRs associated with Biology.
courses.notes: Lab Included | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Cause and Effect; Structure and Function

courses.description: This advanced course is a one-semester continuation of Human Biology, further exploring topics related to human anatomy, physiology, and disease. Topics include: visual physiology and disorders; bones, muscles, joints, and sports injuries; monoclonal antibody therapies; kidneys and excretory system; and stress and the endocrine system. Investigations include eye dissection; working with medical journal literature using PubMed; urinalysis; joint dissection; and a book report on a chosen topic within the field.
courses.prerequisites: Have met the PBGRs associated with Human Biology and teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Cause and Effect; Structure and Function

courses.description: Forensics is a hands-on investigative science and technology course. Students will learn how to observe, collect, analyze, and evaluate evidence found at crime scenes. Topics include: fingerprint analysis; insect life cycles; toxicology; forensic anthropology (bones); blood spatter; DNA analysis; and evidence collection procedures. Crime scene simulations are an important part of the course and require students to put their knowledge into practice.
courses.prerequisites: Recommendation of science teacher.
courses.notes: One Semester; Grades 10-12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Cause and Effect

courses.description: The subject matter for Honors Biology will be similar to Biology, but with more emphasis on Biology from the molecular perspective. This course will provide an expanded laboratory experience, with greater application of scientific processes and experience with scientific writing. In addition, reading from texts and sources outside the regular assigned text will be required.
courses.prerequisites: Recommendation of Integrated Earth Systems Teacher. Students should be in Math 2 or a higher math course their sophomore year.
courses.notes: Lab Included | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Cause and Effect; Structure and Function

courses.description: Students enrolled in this college preparatory class will study the structure, function, and reproduction of cells; biological molecules; genetics; evolution; diversity and classification of organisms; and ecology. Emphasis is placed on an understanding that the structure of a molecule or organism is directly related to its function. Students will develop scientific observation skills and analyze cause and effect relationships.
courses.prerequisites: Have met the PBGRs associate with Integrated Earth Systems and recommendation of science teacher
courses.notes: Lab Included | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Cause and Effect; Structure and Function

courses.description: Survey of Biology provides an overall view of current theories and practices in the life sciences. Students are asked to consider and evaluate their daily experiences. Major areas of study include life, animals and plants, microbes and disease, human biology, reproduction and heredity, ecology and human influence. Emphasis is placed on an understanding that the structure of a molecule or organism is directly related to its function. Students will develop scientific observation skills and analyze cause and effect relationships.
courses.prerequisites: Recommendation of science teacher
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Cause and Effect; Structure and Function

courses.description: This course builds on the environmental concepts explored in Integrated Earth Systems and Biology, offering students an opportunity to deepen their understanding of the natural world. Environmental Studies focuses on exploring the interconnections between biological, ecological, social, legal, economic, and political systems, all through the lens of environmental conservation and sustainability. Students will engage in hands-on experiences and collaborative projects to examine topics such as climate change, biodiversity, conservation, energy systems, and sustainable practices. The course emphasizes designing innovative and sustainable approaches to real-world environmental challenges while fostering creativity and critical thinking. With a focus on teamwork, exploration, and applied learning, this course invites students who are passionate about the environment and eager to contribute to its preservation and stewardship.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of or concurrent enrollment in Biology and teacher recommendation and have met the PBGRs associated with Integrated Earth Systems
courses.notes: One Semester, Grades 10-12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Systems and System Models; Cause and Effect

courses.description: Integrated Earth Systems is a hands-on course that challenges students to make connections amongst the various scientific disciplines while developing their observational, analytical and quantitative skills to better understand the physical world. This course examines each of Earth’s systems, the hydrosphere, geosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere, in the context of our modern environment. Many science skills such as organizing and analyzing laboratory data, taking accurate laboratory measurements, and using the metric system are emphasized and visited throughout the course. This course serves as a foundation to prepare students for future and more advanced science classes.
courses.prerequisites: Recommendation of 8th grade science teacher
courses.notes: Lab Included | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Systems and System Models

courses.course_name: The Vermont Sustainability Project: Fieldwork, Research, and Community Action
courses.description: The Vermont Sustainability Project is a fall semester, two period course that collaborates with VYCC (Vermont Youth Conservation Corp) and other community partners to explore the connection between Vermont’s working landscape and the ongoing social and environmental issues Vermonters are faced with. During the first quarter, students will spend most of their time engaging in activities on the VYCC campus in Richmond, learning about sustainable farming practices, health care shares to combat rural poverty, Vermont’s recreation economy and various conservation topics. During the second quarter, students will participate in many exploratory opportunities through guest speakers and frequent field trips, and will ultimately choose one or more community mentors to develop and carry out a project designed to explore solutions to local social, economic, and/or environmental issues.
courses.notes: One Semester, Grades 11 & 12; listed under the heading 'Grades 11/12 Social Studies/Science Elective'; fall semester, two period course; a table of Science, Social Studies and English PBGRs from which one may be chosen per category follows the description | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Presentation, Collaboration (TS); Inquiry (SS); Systems and System Modeling (SCI) In addition, the second quarter project allows you to choose up to one PBGR from each category below:

courses.description: MMU students will start their 9th grade year with a beginning look at how our world came to be the way it is. This will be done through geographic and historical lenses. Students will learn and practice the skills of social scientists and study how geography connects to the way economic, political, and cultural systems have developed, establishing connections between the ancient world and today. The Geography PBGR will be the primary driver for the course content.
courses.fulfills_text: All ninth grade students will take the following course
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Geography

courses.course_name: 10th Grade Social Studies: Systems of the Modern World, 1750 to the Present Day
courses.description: The world changed dramatically during the 18th and 19th Centuries, bringing in what historians describe as “the modern era.” In 10th grade history, students will explore how this new era came about, as well as the systemic shifts that make it modern. Students examine this concept of modernity through a thematic study of the new political, social, and economic systems that emerged during this period, and explore how our complex contemporary world has both challenged and built upon these ideas of modernity and progress.
courses.fulfills_text: Tenth grade students must take one of the following courses (2020 or 2015)
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Geography; Economics; World Cultures

courses.course_name: 10th Grade Honors Social Studies: Systems of the Modern World, 1750 to the Present Day
courses.description: See 10th Grade Social Studies description. In addition, students examine this concept of modernity through a sophisticated thematic analysis of the new political, social, and economic systems that emerged during this period, and explore how post-war and postcolonial movements have challenged these ideas of modernity and progress through a deeper analysis of data, complex texts, and inquiry. Successful students will bring a strong work ethic and curiosity about history.
courses.prerequisites: 9th grade PBGR met and teacher recommendation.
courses.fulfills_text: Tenth grade students must take one of the following courses (2020 or 2015)
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Geography; Economics; World Cultures

courses.description: Advanced Placement U.S. History is a rigorous year-long course designed to offer a college-level experience. The course covers the range of American history, from pre-discovery through the present, including an overview of significant world events as they influence the development of the country. Students are expected to handle weekly reading and writing assignments on an independent basis. The Advanced Placement program culminates in a national examination in May that could possibly lead to college credit for the course. Students interested in the course should have strong motivation, strong writing skills, an ability to work independently, and a willingness to participate in discussion.
courses.prerequisites: 9th and 10th Grade PBGRs met as well as two teacher recommendations.
courses.notes: Grades 11 & 12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Civics,Government & Society; History; Inquiry

courses.description: In this full-year course, students will examine the social, political, civic, and economic issues that have faced the United States from the origin of the country to the present. The course will use a thematic approach and will cover the foundations of United States government, United States economic history, the immigrant experience, expansion and conflict, social justice and reform. This is a college preparatory course that fulfills proficiency based graduation requirements in Civics, History, and Inquiry. This is a required course for all students except those electing AP U.S. History.
courses.fulfills_text: This is a required course for all students except those electing AP U.S. History.
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Civics,Government & Society; History; Inquiry

courses.description: The purpose of AP World History is to develop a greater understanding of the evolution of global societies over time. The approach is an era based study of what takes place around the world at the same time. This understanding is advanced through a combination of factual knowledge and appropriate analytical skills. The timeframe is from 1000 CE to the present. Areas covered are Europe, Mesoamerica, Asia, Middle East and India. Course highlights: the nature of changes in international frameworks and their causes and consequences as well as comparisons among major societies. A thematic approach is used for this course. As this is an Advanced Placement course, it requires a high commitment on the part of the student.
courses.offering_note: Offered in alternate years from AP US Government & Politics; offered in 2026-27 and then again in 2028-29
courses.notes: Grades 11 & 12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: World Cultures | Note: This course is offered in alternate years from AP US Government & Politics. It will be offered in 2026–27 and then again in the 2028–29 school year.

courses.course_name: Advanced Placement US Government and Politics
courses.description: AP US Government and Politics provides a college-level, analytical introduction to key political concepts, ideas, institutions, and policies that characterize the political culture and government of the United States. How does congress work? Why do we have only two major political parties? What role does the media play in influencing public opinion? What is the Electoral College and why do we have it? We will examine these and many other relevant questions regarding political institutions, processes, and behavior. This class will encourage students to become more effective, engaged citizens as they prepare themselves to be part of an educated electorate. In addition, students will complete a political science research or applied civics project. This is a college preparatory course that will prepare students to take the AP US Government & Politics Exam in May.
courses.offering_note: Not Offered in 2026-27; offered in alternate years from AP World History; next offered in 2027-28
courses.notes: Grades 11 & 12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Civics, Government and Society; Economics | Note: This course is offered in alternate years from AP World History. It is NOT offered in 2026–27; it will be offered next in the 2027-28 school year.

courses.course_name: People in Peril: Exploring Threats We Face
courses.description: We, as humans, face many challenges in the 21st century, both domestically and globally. From climate change driven natural disasters, homelessness, and addiction in Vermont…as well as rising authoritarianism, virus pandemics and war around the world; the threats are plentiful, and in need of recognition and solution. This course is an opportunity to explore some of these challenges through personal inquiry. Students will choose a topic of personal interest, and use the semester to explore the history of, the danger of, and best solutions to address that challenge. Students are encouraged to explore these challenges through a local perspective.
courses.notes: One Semester; Grades 11 & 12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Inquiry

courses.description: Psychology is a course in the science of human behavior. Some of the topics covered are the brain and behavior, human development, theories of personality, dreams, social influences, mental illness and research methods in psychology. This course provides a general overview of the study of Psychology.
courses.notes: One Semester; Grades 11 & 12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Inquiry

courses.description: Students who successfully completed Psychology 1 will further explore topics in psychology such as Sensation & Perception, Motivation & Learning, Memory, Theories of Personality, and Group Dynamics. There will be opportunities to conduct mini experiments and participate in hands-on learning activities.
courses.prerequisites: Psychology
courses.notes: One Semester-Spring; Grades 11 & 12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Inquiry

courses.description: Do billions of dollars in aid to Africa help? How can I tell if a charity is worth donating to? Are big corporations contributing to global poverty and environmental degradation? This course will examine the efforts to develop the “Third World” through questions like these and an examination of issues like fast fashion and sweatshop labor, climate change and sustainability, corporate social responsibility and certifications, human trafficking and rights for all. Students will learn the scope of issues facing the world, grapple with the different strategies being employed, and focus on a particular area of interest to make a change. Want to help make the world a better place? Learn how!
courses.notes: One Semester; Grades 10-12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Economics

courses.description: This is the study of human society and human relationships. This course will focus on how the discipline of sociology examines society and human behavior in social settings. The course covers the major concepts of culture and social groups, and how people are socialized by family, peers, school, and the media. It also explores the topics of crime/deviance, the criminal justice system, and race/racism. Students will be expected to question social norms, reflect on their upbringings, and examine the structures and institutions that define our society. They will also conduct sociological research on a question they want to find out the answer to.
courses.notes: One Semester; Grades 11 & 12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Inquiry

courses.description: Economics is the science of choice: the choices people make as they seek to satisfy their wants in a world of scarcity. In Economics, we will focus on how we make those choices, both financial and social choices, and what the societal outcomes of our collective choices on national, state, and global levels. Students will explore various economic concepts and systems along with exploring economic interdependence in a globalized economy. This will include environmental impacts, poverty, global development, political relationships and more. The insights economic reasoning provide us are powerful, and can help us understand human behavior, make more informed personal choices and make sense of current events in a complex world.
courses.notes: One Semester; Grades 10-12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Economics

courses.description: This course will focus on a variety of areas of the law including Criminal Law, Constitutional Law, and Civil Law. Individual liberties found in the Bill of Rights will be covered, including freedom of speech, search and seizure, right to bear arms, and equal protection of the laws. Students will gain an understanding of how the court system operates, including trial courts and appellate courts. The course will take a hands-on approach in which students will conduct mock trials, mock appellate arguments, and a variety of role-plays. Guest speakers and field trips on various law-related topics will help bring a real world perspective to the course. This course serves as a foundation for students interested in participating in the Vermont High School Mock Trial Competition.
courses.notes: Grades 11 & 12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Civics, Government and Society

courses.description: We will examine the nature, development, and role of terror and terrorist groups in a modern context. This examination will compare and contrast the origins, actions, and current situations through a mix of the following movements: Tamil Tigers in Sri Lanka, Irish Republican Army of Ireland, Maoist Rebels of Nepal, White Nationalist Movements in the U.S., Left Wing U.S. Domestic Terror, and Western Asian Terror (Al Qaeda, ISIS, etc). This course will attempt to understand the motivations behind terror as a tactic. Through the study and understanding of common roots of terror activity, we will discuss foreign policy solutions that may prevent the seeds of terrorism from germinating.
courses.notes: One Semester; Grades 10-12 | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: World Cultures

courses.description: In this first year course, basic language skills are introduced. Students develop a basic knowledge of French language, vocabulary, grammar and culture while working on the proficiencies of Interpretive Listening and Reading, Interpersonal Speaking and Writing, and Cultural Practices.

The second course continues the emphasis on the language skills of listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Students review and expand vocabulary and grammar from French 1. We continue to develop a knowledge of French language and culture while working on the proficiencies of Interpretive Listening and Reading, Interpersonal Speaking and Writing, and Cultural Practices. The amount of French used in class increases throughout the year.
courses.prerequisites: French 1 and teacher recommendation.

courses.description: This course focuses on integrating the proficiencies of listening, speaking, reading, and writing, while encouraging students to begin to “think” in French. Students will be able to sustain conversations on selected topics using a variety of tenses. Students work towards deeper listening/reading comprehension and expanded writing skills. This class is conducted predominantly in French.
courses.prerequisites: French 2 and teacher recommendation.

courses.description: In this course, students prepare for AP French as they show mastery of the proficiencies in their ability to understand and discuss the main ideas of both factual and abstract topics, express and support opinions and preferences, and request clarification of misunderstood information. Students read a variety of texts in modern, conversational, and journalistic French, as well as French literature. Students prepare oral and written reports, and concentrate on mastering selective vocabulary and advanced grammar. Students will be aware of and discuss current life, events, and trends in the Francophone world. This course is conducted entirely in French.
courses.prerequisites: French 3 and teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Global Citizenship–World Cultures

courses.description: Students will fine-tune their French language proficiencies through a study of culture, literature, grammar and vocabulary. This four-skills course (listening, speaking, reading, and writing) is taught in themes and contexts provided by the College Board and serves as a highly challenging preparation for the French Language AP Examination. The class is conducted entirely in French.
courses.prerequisites: French 4 and teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Global Citizenship–World Cultures

courses.description: In Spanish 1 students learn basic vocabulary and grammatical structures, as well as how to hold a simple conversation. Students develop an introductory knowledge of Spanish language and culture while working on the proficiencies of Interpretive Listening and Reading, Interpersonal Speaking and Writing, and Cultural Practices. Students explore Hispanic culture through a variety of projects and instructional methods.

In Spanish 2 students revisit vocabulary, skills and grammatical structures from level one and learn new skills such as how to talk in the past tense. Spanish 2 is an extension of the first year. Students continue learning how to listen, read, write and speak in Spanish. The amount of Spanish used in class increases throughout the year. Students participate in conversation, explore art and culture and play games.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish 1 and teacher recommendation.

courses.description: This course focuses on integrating the proficiencies of listening, speaking, reading, and writing, while encouraging students to begin to “think” in Spanish. Students will be able to sustain conversations on selected topics using a variety of tenses. Students work towards deeper listening/reading comprehension and expanded writing skills. This class is conducted predominantly in Spanish.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish 2 and teacher recommendation.

courses.description: In this course, students prepare for AP Spanish as they show mastery of the proficiencies in their ability to understand and discuss the main ideas of both factual and abstract topics, express and support opinions and preferences, and request clarification of misunderstood information. Students read a variety of texts in modern, conversational and journalistic Spanish. Students prepare oral and written reports, and concentrate on mastering selective vocabulary and advanced grammar. Students will be aware of and discuss current life, events, and trends in the Hispanic world. This course is conducted entirely in Spanish.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish 3 and teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Global Citizenship–World Cultures

courses.description: Students will fine-tune their Spanish language proficiencies through a study of culture, literature, grammar and vocabulary. This four-skills course (listening, speaking, reading, and writing) is taught in themes and contexts provided by the College Board and serves as a highly challenging preparation for the Spanish Language and Culture AP Examination. The class is conducted entirely in Spanish.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish 4 and teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Global Citizenship–World Cultures

courses.description: Welcome to the dynamic and challenging world of business. This course is designed for students seeking a non-traditional classroom experience and anyone interested in taking control of their learning. Working as a member of a team you will be actively engaged in business management and challenged to relate theories to your experience. Reading, writing, and reflecting are all critical parts of this course. You will learn how to manage yourself and your co-workers in a classroom designed for risk taking. You MUST be willing to lead and should not expect to sit quietly through instruction. Students will leave this course better prepared for life after high school by immersing in a year-long case study of workplace dynamics. You will work both within and outside of your skill sets and you will learn more from your peers than you may think possible. Be prepared to challenge yourself and your classmates, and above all else come ready to think. Recommended for any student who is a passionate and excited learner. Ideal for those planning to major in Business or Psychology, or considering owning or managing a business, although theories apply to all aspects of life.
courses.prerequisites: Junior or senior standing or by permission of teacher.
courses.notes: Prerequisite states junior or senior standing or permission of teacher

courses.description: This course will teach the basics of design and production of wood products. The course will focus on learning skills, safety, and the practical knowledge required to work with hand and power tools. Topics include: project planning, construction, finishing methods, wood technology and joining methods. The qualities of good design will be expressed by your own creative application of the techniques of woodworking.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Visual Arts
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: Creating art is at the core of the Introduction to Visual Arts course; no previous art experience is necessary. This one semester foundation course will introduce students to basic foundational art skills and their own sense of creativity through a variety of media and techniques. Students explore both two dimensional (flat) and three dimensional (sculptural) art forms while learning about the visual language of art.
courses.notes: One Semester; Introduction to Visual Arts is a prerequisite for all visual arts classes that assess proficiency based graduation requirements

courses.description: Artists will learn about the process of 2D design and observational drawing and painting as projects are sequentially designed promoting critical thinking and encouraging individual expression and imagination. This course allows students to express themselves and communicate visually. As students explore this means of creative communication, they acquire more problem solving skills. Students do not need drawing or painting experience to take this course. The course explores drawing and painting from observation and imagination using a variety of media including: pencil, charcoal, colored pencils, pastels, watercolors, liquid watercolors, acrylic paint and various mediums. Artists study the characteristics of value, color and color mixing and learn about composition, space, light, and form in order to create successful drawings and paintings. A variety of drawing and painting methods will be explored.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Visual Arts
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: This course builds upon the skills gained in the Drawing and Painting 1 class with the focus of creating more complex and unique pieces of art. Students will have a chance to work in a self-paced, independent environment with support from the instructor to help build upon skills learned in the previous term. Students will be encouraged to explore media and methods of their choice.
courses.prerequisites: Drawing/Painting 1
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: This Graphic Arts and Design course will focus on how artists use visual literacy to create dynamic works of art that are both aesthetically appealing and have compelling visual imagery that we see everyday in the world around us, from the clothes we wear, the music we listen to, the books we read, the cars we drive, and much more. By learning about how graphic designers use typography (lettering forms) as well as compositional considerations to create logos, labels, posters, album covers, etc. and combine that knowledge with how graphic artists create artwork that utilize several types of 2D media, such as drawing, painting, vinyl stickers, printmaking and silk screening on textiles, students will create several concepts and bring their ideas to a visually satisfying conclusion for a wide audience. Students will also be given the opportunity to develop an understanding of the Adobe Creative Suite programs, such as Illustrator and Photoshop. Historical context of the development of design will be addressed through presentations and projects. Graphic Design and Graphic Arts skills are transferable to other areas of a student’s education as well as many aspects of various career choices.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Visual Arts
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: In Graphic Arts and Design 2, students will be challenged to build upon previous knowledge gained in Graphic Design I or Graphic Arts and Design I. Expectations of the students will be raised to create more sophisticated imagery and use more advanced decision-making around the concepts of design. By building on the skills learned in the previous term, students will be encouraged to use their graphic art and design skills to create artwork that will be used in a graphic project such as an advertisement, album or book jacket cover, etc. and also find a “client” who will “commission” them to create art for a specific project. Students will experiment with digital imaging and use Adobe Creative Suite programs and printmaking skills, such as silk screening as well as the vinyl sticker maker to create actual products. Students will also focus on creating a professional portfolio of their work and a final presentation of their learning and skill building will be required.
courses.prerequisites: Graphic Design 1 or Graphic Arts & Design 1
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: In this course students study the tools, equipment and techniques used when working with fine metals. The students learn about the principles of design, metallurgy of fine metals, and the techniques/skills needed to create unique pieces of jewelry and small sculptures. The primary materials used in class are sterling silver, nickel, brass and copper.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Visual Arts
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: This course builds upon the skills gained in the Fine Metals 1 class with the focus of creating more complex and unique pieces of jewelry and sculptures. Students will have a chance to work in a self-paced, independent environment with support from the instructor to help build upon skills learned in the previous term. Students will be encouraged to explore their own styles and approaches as they learn all aspects of the design process. Students will explore a variety of topics such as, forming metal with the use of stakes and hammers, chain construction, and metal finishes. The primary materials used in class are sterling silver, nickel, brass and copper.
courses.prerequisites: Fine Metals 1
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: This course will introduce students to the processes, techniques, and artistry of both digital photography as well as black and white darkroom photography. Students will learn how to use both DSLR (Digital single-lense reflex) and analog 35mm film cameras. Students will learn how to control exposure manually, develop negatives, and create prints in the darkroom, as well as learn the basics of the Adobe Creative Suite, including Adobe Lightroom to edit their photographs and Adobe Photoshop to edit, layer and apply unique effects to their photographs. As they complete assignments, students will become familiar with the different qualities of light and composition tools that give images visual impact and allow photographers to express themselves. The knowledge and skills they gain in class can be easily transferred to other editing programs. With each project, students will build confidence in their photographic ability to take well-composed images and in their expressive creativity by developing photos in both the ‘digital darkroom’ and a ‘real darkroom’. Historical context of the development of photography will be addressed through presentations and projects. With parental permission, students may sign out cameras through the library.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Visual Arts
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: This course is designed to give students advanced instruction and experience with both DSLR and analog 35 mm film cameras. Students will challenge themselves to shoot in difficult lighting situations using flash, making more refined prints, and manually manipulating their prints in the darkroom for black and white film, as well as using Adobe Creative Suite to edit their digital photographs. Photo assignments at this level are presented as “visual problems” to be solved using the skills and techniques mastered in Photography I. Students will be challenged to use their photographs as modes of expression and communication, and will often be free to choose their own subject matter and artistic approach. This course is also designed to cater to the student who would like to work more in-depth from the rest of the class and will have independence but would coincide with the curriculum. Students may sign out cameras in the library for the semester.
courses.prerequisites: Photography 1 or Darkroom Photography 1 (or with permission from the instructor -- Digital Photography)
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: Pottery I is a course that focuses on the art and skills of working with clay, various pottery tools, and glazes. Pottery I students will learn a basic vocabulary for the medium in order to build their artistic literacy within a relaxed, creative, and productive learning environment. Historical context of the development of design will be addressed through presentations and projects in order for students to gain a deeper understanding of the medium as well as an appreciation for this ancient art form. Students will become proficient in hand building as well as have a chance to learn how to use the pottery wheel. Developing craftsmanship and an aesthetic eye are two of the goals.
courses.prerequisites: Introduction to Visual Arts
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: Pottery 2 is a course for students who have become passionate about the art of ceramics. Students will have a chance to work in a self-paced, independent environment with support from the instructor to help build upon skills learned in the previous term. Both handbuilding and pottery wheel techniques will be encouraged, and students will be supported to take risks with their learning in a relaxed, creative, and productive learning environment. Pottery 2 students will also be required to study a potter or a ceramicist of their own choosing in order to build on their knowledge of this artform and to be inspired in their own art making.
courses.prerequisites: Pottery 1
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: This course is intended for motivated art students who are willing to devote considerable time and effort to the development and submission of an Advanced Placement Studio Art portfolio to the College Board. During the fall, the artists will experiment with a variety of approaches and media to show evidence of a breadth of experiences. In the process, the students’ artwork should acquire a sense of quality and variety. AP artists will also begin to develop a concentrated focus on individual artistic concerns. In the spring, students will continue this in-depth exploration of a specific visual idea. Substantial time will need to be spent on work outside of the classroom in order to create the quantity and quality of work necessary for an impressive AP portfolio. Participation in discussing and viewing students’ and masters’ work will be mandatory.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of two first level visual art courses or portfolio review performed by the teacher
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: This course is a performing group with special emphasis on the developing musician. Students will learn and practice basic skills such as sight-reading, intonation, rhythm, counting, scales, arpeggios and a wide variety of repertoire. A highly anticipated Marching Band season opens the first quarter, and for the remainder of the year we combine to perform three to four concerts as a full Symphonic Band. All performances are required assessments, and students are also graded with audio or video submissions for artistic literacy (Playing) and reflections before, during and after performances. Band is a wonderful way to work with a large, inviting group of students and to have fun learning while preparing for concerts and other performances. Students are encouraged to audition for various music festivals such as the District, All-State, and New England music festivals and will have many other opportunities to further their playing. Artistic literacy and reflection critique proficiency assessments will be evaluated throughout the year.
courses.prerequisites: Basic instrumental proficiency
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: The string instrument is vital to quality music worldwide. Emphasis in this class is on exposure to music of many styles. There will be some selections combining the strings for full orchestra with woodwinds, brass and percussion. All performances are required assessments, and students are also graded with audio or video submissions for artistic literacy (Playing) and reflections before, during and after performances. Three to four school concerts will be performed yearly and are required. There are also opportunities available for students to audition for music performance festivals. Artistic literacy and reflection critique proficiency assessments will be evaluated throughout the year.
courses.prerequisites: Basic instrumental proficiency
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: Wind Ensemble is an audition or teacher recommendation only ensemble open to all instrumentalists in grades 10–12. Instrumental musicianship, combined with ensemble methods, is used to build a strong music organization that enables adaptation to different playing situations. This class utilizes more of the musicality that is needed to play advanced repertoire. A highly anticipated Marching Band season opens the first quarter, and for the remainder of the year we perform three to four concerts as a full ensemble. Members are expected to participate in a music festival; Northwest District music festival, All State Music Festival or the New England Music Festival. Students who decide to participate in the New England festival will need sponsorship through a private teacher and/or parent as the MMU instrumental department will not be sponsoring this event. Wind Ensemble is a yearlong commitment and students are expected to participate for the full year and are required to be at all performances. Artistic literacy and reflection critique proficiency assessments will be evaluated throughout the year.
courses.prerequisites: Audition or recommendation by teacher AND show proficiency in both the Artistic Literacy PBGRs (Artistic Literacy and Reflection and Critique)
courses.notes: open to all instrumentalists in grades 10-12; audition or teacher recommendation only | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: Designed for singers of all experience levels, students are given the opportunity to work together as a team and build confidence in singing and in performance. Through this class students will gain vital skills in intonation, diction, breathing, tone production, range, harmony, understanding rhythm, sight-reading, and phrasing. This class is also an important performance opportunity. Students perform four concerts a year; in which attendance is mandatory for grading purposes. Missed concerts will result in an alternative assignment to make up for the missed concert grade. Musical selections range through all choral genres. Auditions for District, All States, and New England festivals are also available. Artistic literacy and reflection critique proficiency assessments will be evaluated during the second semester. This course is required for participation in all co-curricular choirs (Lower Voices Chorus, Select Chorus and Madrigal Singers).
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.course_name: Advanced Placement Music Theory and Composition
courses.description: This course is designed for students who have gained facility with the basic concepts of musical notation and harmonic analysis. This is a course designed to further student’s study of scores, composition, and harmonic progression. This course will prepare those who wish to take the Advanced Placement Exam in Music Theory for success. Students will be required to compose four pieces over the course of the school year on the web-based notation program Noteflight, as well as a continuation of ear training, voice leading & four-part writing, score and harmonic analysis, the history of Western Music, melodic and harmonic dictation.
courses.prerequisites: Musical performance, experience and desire to learn music in greater depth and breadth
courses.notes: Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: This course is designed to appeal to students coming from various musical backgrounds and is a springboard to greater understanding of music. Basic concepts include: tuning, meter, rhythm, notation, composition, and improvisation. The chromatic, major, minor, pentatonic and blues scales with their formulas are taught as well as first position and barred chords. Playing written melodies, strumming, picking techniques and a brief history of the guitar are covered. Students will be supplied the text for reference and continued use. Course concentrates on acoustic guitar.
courses.notes: One Semester | Note: Students must provide their own acoustic guitars.

courses.description: Advanced guitar is offered for students seeking an in-depth experience in guitar playing. A variety of music will be studied that guides students into deeper aspects of Jazz, Blues, Rock, and Classical guitar performance. Students will study reading and playing technique in 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 5th, and 7th positions, harmonics, fingerstyle and strumming, learning and gaining facility improvising and playing music on the entire fretboard. Students will perform in various forms alone and with others for audiences and for the instructor music of various genres and cultures.
courses.prerequisites: Beginning guitar class or proficiency, comfort and facility with reading notation in 1st position on the guitar/teacher permission.
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: This class is offered for beginners. Basic concepts are taught, such as meter, rhythm, form and notation. Playing written music, composing simple songs, improvising, following chord charts and playing by ear are all part of the curriculum. Weekly small recitals and written assignments provide structured goals and opportunity for assessment even though everyone progresses at their own individual pace. Students are encouraged to purchase the two lesson and theory books for reference and continued use.
courses.notes: One Semester

courses.description: This class is offered for the student who completed Basic Piano and has previous piano experience. Level 2 continues to progress smoothly and easily, without gaps, toward the development of technique and knowledge required to play in all the most frequently used keys. Weekly recitals provide structured goals and opportunity for assessment even though everyone progresses at their own individual pace. Students are encouraged to purchase the Adult All-In-One Course Level 2 book.
courses.notes: One Semester | Proficiency Based Graduation Requirement Assessed: Artistic Literacy; Reflection and Critique

courses.description: The focus of Driver Education is to assist students in developing responsible driving skills, habits, knowledge, and attitudes with an emphasis on safety and respect for all roadway users. Students are enrolled once their permit is on file in student services according to their birth date with older students being served first because enrollment is limited. Students should have a study hall scheduled to allow for the driving lab. Each student is state mandated to receive 30 hours of classroom instruction, six hours of in-car instruction, and six hours of in-car observation. Students must also complete an informational traffic safety project and 20 hours of documented practice driving with parents or other adults. Students must have successfully completed all work with an 80% or better as well as pass the final drive test with an 80% or better before a completion certificate is issued. Students will be removed from the course if they are cited for motor vehicle, alcohol or drug violations. See Driver Education Procedures for additional information.
courses.prerequisites: 10th grade status and a copy of permit on file in Student Services.
courses.notes: One Semester; prerequisite states 10th grade status

courses.description: As outlined in Vermont law (16 V.S.A. § 131), this full year 9th grade required comprehensive health education course will cover a variety of learning experiences defined as the core concepts. This includes the study of Body Structure and Function, Community Health, Safety, Disease, Family and Mental Health, Personal health habits, Human Development, Consumer health, Drugs and Alcohol, Nutrition and How to recognize and prevent sexual abuse and violence. Skills addressed include interpersonal communication, goal setting and decision-making, accessing information, analyzing influences, advocacy, and self management. Students will also engage in a variety of physical activities including self-defense, ultimate Frisbee, dance, adventure ropes course, mountain biking, and personal fitness. Students must have an appropriate change of clothes for participation in activity
